label: Heating sealed containers
summary: Heat a closed container and what's inside expands or boils until it bursts, throwing hot contents, metal or glass. Aerosols, gas cylinders, unopened food tins, glass jars, drums and a fireplace water heater whose flow has stopped all do it, and a drum that looks empty can hold residue that explodes.
signs: Aerosol cans of any kind, such as cooking spray and cleaners: labels read CONTENTS UNDER PRESSURE and CONTAINER MAY EXPLODE IF HEATED
Gas cylinders and canisters of every size: containers may explode when heated, and ruptured cylinders may rocket; see Compressed gas
Unopened food tins, and glass jars, near a stove, oven, grill or fire
Drums, cans and tanks that look empty but may hold fuel or chemical residue in their seams and folds
A fireplace water heater (a steel grate or liner piped into a home hot-water heating system): if the circulator pump fails, the power fails or a pipe freezes, the water inside can boil into steam
Rubbish or scrap headed for a burn barrel, fire pit, stove or furnace with cans or closed containers mixed in
do: Open food tins before heating them, take the label off first, and lift hot tins with tongs or heat-resistant gloves

Keep aerosols and cylinders away from stoves, heaters, grills and other heat: an aerosol of cooking oil on a shelf 53 cm (21 in) above a hot griddle burst and put a kitchen worker in hospital for several days with serious burns
Pick aerosols, gas canisters, tins, jars and other closed containers out of anything you are going to burn

Fit a safety (pressure relief) valve in the outlet pipe as close as possible to a fireplace water heater, with no valves or restrictions between them, and trip it now and then to check it, keeping clear of the hot water

If a cylinder or tank is in a fire, get everyone well back and stay away. The ERG gives 1600 m (1 mile) all round for a flammable-gas tank, rail tank car or tank truck in a fire, and 800 m (1/2 mile) for compressed or liquefied gas tanks
Leave at once if a heated cylinder's relief valve gets louder or the tank changes colour
If a drum must be cut, use cold cutting such as hydraulic shears or a pneumatic chisel, not a torch, welding, a grinder or a disc cutter; HSE notes hot work often isn't needed at all
dont: Don't put aerosols, gas canisters, sealed tins or jars in a burn barrel, fire pit or stove: they can explode, and an exploding aerosol can throws debris that injures people and can light nearby vegetation
Don't heat, puncture or burn an aerosol: those are its label's own warnings
Don't heat an unopened tin, and don't put mason jars in an oven: they aren't tempered and can explode
Don't fire a fireplace water heater unless water can flow through it and a working relief valve is fitted
Don't torch-cut, weld, grind or disc-cut a drum or container that held fuel, oil or anything unknown: residue can explode, and workers have been killed cutting drums
ppe: Safety glasses or goggles, with a face shield over them, when working near heated containers; a face shield alone doesn't stop impact
Tongs or heat-resistant gloves for hot tins and pots
Against a cylinder or tank in a fire, distance is the protection: the ERG says always stay away from tanks in contact with flames
firstAid: Burns and scalds: cool under cool running water for 20 minutes; take clothing and jewellery off the burned area, but leave anything stuck to the skin
Cover with cling film or a clean cloth, with no ice, creams or oil; burns bigger than a large coin, or on the face, hands, feet, joints or groin, need medical care
Cuts from metal or glass fragments: see Sharp edges, and don't pull out pieces that are deeply stuck
Breathed gas from a burst can or cylinder: get to fresh air; see Compressed gas
